prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints tied to asset values amplify and propagate shocks, giving a dynamic theory of credit cycles.

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is the cleanest attribution problem on the shortlist. It is a single, identifiable two-author mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values link credit to asset prices, so small shocks become large and persistent. The mechanism is conceptually fundamental, and it carries real weight because a large quantitative literature on financial frictions, intermediaries and macroprudential policy is built on it. About three decades have passed, so its influence has been tested in theory, calibrated models and post-2008 policy analysis. Beyond macro-finance, the amplification logic is used in growth, development and firm-dynamics models where credit constraints interact with productivity and reallocation, which is the part I know best. I judge candidates by the same criteria across fields: a crisp discovery, clear credit, durable influence and time for confirmation. B007 meets all four more cleanly than the broader candidates, where credit is spread over many names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is thematic overlap with the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig, since the financial accelerator and banking-crisis literature are close relatives. A second concern is that the empirical identification of collateral channels is less clean than the theory, so a committee that weights direct empirical confirmation may rate the work as more theoretical than some rivals. Finally, B007 has narrower cross-field appeal than B026 and B012, which I do not count as merit but which affects whether it can carry a majority.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B007 second, calls it a clear and original contribution cleanly attributable to Kiyotaki and Moore, but flags overlap with the 2022 prize and the fact that the financial-accelerator strand is not captured by two names.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and I take the overlap concern seriously, but I think it is smaller than it looks. The 2022 prize recognised bank runs, deposit insurance and the role of bank failures in the Great Depression. Kiyotaki-Moore is a different mechanism: a dynamic general-equilibrium feedback between collateral values and borrowing, with no bank run or intermediary failure required. I would not try to cover the accelerator strand by widening the prize. That strand is the part tied to Bernanke's already-recognised work, and widening it blurs the discovery.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B007 first and proposes adding Mark Gertler as a third laureate, for the financial accelerator and intermediary-frictions extensions, while acknowledging the overlap with Bernanke's earlier prize and Gertler's credit under B012.
responses.response: We agree on the core, and I see the case for Gertler's contribution to quantitative financial-friction models. I still prefer the two-name version. The accelerator is closely tied to Bernanke, who is outside this ballot entry and already a laureate, so adding Gertler raises exactly the attribution question the pair avoids. Gertler's credit is also contested between B007 and B012, and I would not want the committee to commit it twice. If the committee wants a broader macro-finance prize, Gertler is the natural third name. I would present that as a deliberate widening, not as the default.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B012 first as the foundation of modern central-bank practice, but ranks B007 sixth because of overlap with earlier recognition of Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig and because the committee may want more direct empirical confirmation of the specific mechanism.
responses.response: Andersson is right that the policy footprint of the New Keynesian framework is very large, and I ranked B012 fourth for that reason. My difficulty is attribution: eight credited names and several distinct strands (Calvo pricing, Taylor contracts and rule, Woodford's synthesis, Gali, and the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Smets estimation line) mean any three-person cut leaves out contributors the committee would regard as essential. On empirical confirmation, I accept that collateral channels are harder to identify than the model suggests. The mechanism has still proved useful as the organising device for crisis-era work and for models of financial frictions. That is influence on how the field reasons, and it does not depend on a single decisive test.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B026 first, crediting Melitz and Helpman, and treats Redding's quantitative extensions as more derivative of the original framework. She also notes the 2008 trade prize does not cover this advance.
responses.response: I agree that Melitz (2003) is the anchor and that Redding's contribution is more of an extension, and B026 is my own second choice. I would put weight on the parallel Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line, which is not credited on this ballot entry. The committee would have to explain why Helpman rather than those contributors is the second name. That attribution question is why I still prefer B007, where the two-author credit has no obvious missing claimant. I would regard B026 as a strong prize if the committee is comfortable with that explanation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as disqualifying or as complementary.
Whether the committee prefers a two-name prize or a wider macro-finance prize that adds Gertler, and Gilchrist if the accelerator is to be covered.
How the committee weights theoretical influence against direct empirical identification of collateral channels.
Whether the right second name for B026 is Helpman or a contributor from the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line, which affects how I rank B026 against B007.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the credited candidates on B007 is apparent from my profile. I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and a co-author of John Hassler (chair), and I am a colleague of both at the IIES, but neither is a candidate. My long-running collaboration with Klenow and Aghion concerns work not on this shortlist, and my professional proximity to growth and firm-dynamics research could bias my sense of B026's relevance.
